questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
1) Being able to receive the Erasmus scholarship.
2) A good university with interesting courses.
3) A large variety of courses taught in English - this turned out to be surprisingly limited in the EU.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: TUM is great at keeping incoming students updated and informed on how they run their university, e.g. deadlines, how to navigate in student platform, etc. Overall it was very well done and I felt confident and unworried about administrative things all the time there.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
All the assistance I needed was provided without me needing to ask for it. Information meetings, intro days with other students at TUM, general walkthrough of the exam system and how to "normally" attend courses. 
Even before arriving, TUM offered much service as to what courses to choose, how and when this should be done, etc. 
The only assistance I reached out for has been for signatures and stamps on official documents for Erasmus and credit transfer to my home university. I think it helps a lot that TUM is such a big university.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Munich is notoriously hard to find accommodation in. Even so, TUM still had some contacts that they were able to forward for housing off campus. This was a great service, but I ended up finding somewhere through an online portal,
wg-gesucht.de
, broadly used by people seeking housing in Munich. I can recommend people to set up a contact advertisement on
wg-gesucht.de
. Often landlords are overwhelmed by the interest on their housing advertisement that sometimes hundreds of people react to. Instead of writing on a lot of these advertisements you can make your own advertisement in there with your budget and other requirements, making it likely for landlords themselves to reach out to you.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Living off campus was ideal for me. TUM Informatics is situated 40 minutes away from city centre in the metro, so chances are you won't be spending so much time in Munich if you choose to live on campus. Garching city by the campus is quite small and boring, so my bets are you'd be missing out on the opportunities in Munich. If you plan on taking language courses, classes will take place in Munich city.
Also, if you choose to live on campus in a dorm, you should be aware that language barrier is a thing with your roommates, unless you speak German well. Local students will quickly switch to German if standing with other local students, leaving you feeling kind of left out. 
However, living off campus is generally also considerably more expensive as you probably won't be living in a dorm.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
Having received and accepted the nomination from my sending institution, I simply had to transfer a fee 


TUM processed my application documents. I soon received an e-mail with the decision that I had been accepted. 
Then, I had to complete the enrollment steps for TUM that included transferring a fee of 152,2 euros and a proof of health insurance. It was enough to have my European health insurance card (det blå sygesikringskort) verified by a German health insurance provider - please do this in good time!

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I was sent many thorough guides explaining how to complete each steps and several reminders. This was a great help to me and I never had to reach out to get additional information. TUM has 1-2 persons that are responsible for incoming Erasmus students that you are always able to reach out to, if needed.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
TUM Informatics has some different types of classes: 
1) Praktikum: practical courses where you apply theoretical knowledge to a concrete problem. Very popular and small capacity for each course.
2) Seminar: theoretical courses where you explore latest developments within a field and present your findings. Also very popular and small capacity for each course.
3) Lecture: classic style course where you attend lectures (and sometimes a few practical classes). Popular but rarely have capacity limits.
Then I also took language courses at main campus. 
1), 2) and language courses are very popular, making it difficult to get a spot. I managed to get a spot on my 4th priority of praktikum and 2/3rd priority for seminar. I got all the lecture courses I applied for.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If there is a course you would very much like to attend, please reach out to the course responsible person. They want engaged and excited students, so they might be able to get you a spot, even if you did not get one through the system. Perhaps even showing up to the first classes also gets you a spot, which happened to someone at my German class since some registered people did not show up for the first class, leaving an empty spot.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I think the level was appropriate. Praktikums and Seminars are very popular partly because lectures can be difficult to pass, since the exams often are very short and demanding when Praktikums and Seminars typically are graded based on a final report and presentation. 
I do not think I would have passed all credits if I had only taken lecture courses. 
However, in general teaching was great. The professors are very skilled and generally good educators.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching at DIKU is very set in stone. It is not often that courses are taught in different ways, and when they are it is as a blow of fresh air. Usually we have lectures, classes and weekly/bi-weekly handins in all courses. It was great to experience something else to switch it up.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Requirements Engineering, Security Engineering, Master-Praktikum - Machine Learning in Crowd Modeling & Simulation, Advanced Seminar Blockchain Technologies, German as a Foreign Language A1.1, English - Academic Presentation Skills C1 - C2

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
1) Language courses! It is always fun to learn a new language and you meet a lot of other people that you can make friends with. 
2) Advanced Seminar Blockchain Technologies. A great course for diving more into the new developments within blockchain technology, even making your own implementation if that's what you are interested in. 
3)  English - Academic Presentation Skills C1 - C2. I become very nervous when presenting but this course helped me deal with it a little better.

questions.answer: None.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Eating out is cheaper, but generally Munich is as costly as Copenhagen in most regards except public transportation that became very cheap when the Deutschland ticket was introduced. Also, the TUM student card allows you to travel for free in weekdays 18-06 and all day in weekends.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Unfortunately the sports club was in all German and the spots were sold out within limits. Generally, it was one of the few things that there was not a lot of information about. 
This was in great contrast to the social and cultural events that were many and varied, thanks to TUMi and MENSA! TUMi and MENSA arranged hiking trips, dance lessons, parties, city rallies, and many other things.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Please go to all the TUMi and MENSA events that you can muster. You meet so many great people there and uncover hidden gems only otherwise known to locals.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Also, here are so many great spots to visit in the region and they are all worth a visit. Such as Königssee, Zugspitze, Eibsee, Salzburg, Landshut, Nürnberg, Regensburg - and many more!
Trips are arranged by the student societies MENSA and TUMi, but once you get to know people it is also very easy to just tag along or finding others to go with with the Deutschland ticket, which makes it very cheap to explore the region.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
It was very easy. Germany is not that different from Denmark. Munich specifically even focuses on introducing more biking culture, making it feel even more like Copenhagen. 
I will miss hanging out with my friends in the bier gartens.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
You can meet and socialize with local students:
1) when doing group work in seminars and praktikums
2) joining the sports clubs (which I had no luck doing)
3) moving into a dorm

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: In all honesty, none. Munich is a little more conservative, but it was not something that I really noticed.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I loved that people often went hiking in the weekend. In this region there are many beautiful mountains, forests and lakes. Particularly for the mountains there is the whole Austrian-like culture with small huts and eating kaiserschmarrn after a long hike.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) It will most likely be stressful to sort out housing, but always remember it will work out in the end!
2) Be up front if you want to go for a specific course, do not hold yourself back. Go talk to the professor and see if you can get a spot! Registration for exams is very late so it is possible to change courses late. 
3) Go take a swim in the Eisbach and chill with a beer and bretzen. It is an absolute iconic experience when going to Munich. 
4) Go to all the TUMi and MENSA events you can muster.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The academic level of courses is less tough as compared to DIKU, so please allow yourself to spend some time enjoying life, the people you are there with and all the experiences that are offered to you when there. But please make sure you study well for the lecture, closed books exams!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed attending courses that were different in both teaching style and content as compared to DIKU. It also made me appreciate my academic background as I felt very well prepared to participate in the teachings, group work and exams.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: There really were no challenges out of the ordinary. Of course you can struggle a bit with course material sometimes, wish you went on that hike to that beautiful, that you studied better for an exam or did not drink that extra beer yesterday, but I can't say that I was really challenged. Word of caution: the smallest beer from tap is half a liter and not .33.

questions.answer: Yes
